original_question: Prove that for any compact analytic two-dimensional Riemannian manifold with analytic boundary, the set of generalized minimal flows is nonempty and is a proper subset of the Yudovich space.
target_in_paper: Section 6.3, Problem 13 (“An attractor of 2D Euler equations and its semianalytic structure”). Your draft is essentially targeting the paper’s official formulation: prove that for any compact analytic Riemannian 2-manifold M with analytic boundary, the set GM(M) of generalized minimal flows is a nonempty proper subset of the Yudovich space YU(M). This is clearly the relevant target rather than Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3, which belong to a different part of the paper. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
correct_elements: The draft already gets the main claim almost exactly right: it has the correct ambient setting (compact analytic two-dimensional Riemannian manifold with analytic boundary), the correct object of interest (generalized minimal flows), and the correct conclusion (that these form a nonempty proper subset of the Yudovich space). In substance, it is very close to Problem 13 itself. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
missing_details: It does not define the Yudovich space YU(M). In Section 6.3, YU(M) consists of divergence-free vector fields u on M such that curl u belongs to L∞(M). ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

It does not define a generalized minimal flow. By Definition 6.7, u ∈ YU(M) is a GM-flow if for every w in the weak H^1(M)-closure of its Euler orbit, one has ||curl w||L2(M) = ||curl u||L2(M). ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

It omits the dynamical notation used in the definition: the Euler equations induce a one-parameter group S_t on YU(M); O(u) is the orbit of u under S_t; and \bar O(u) is the weak closure of O(u) in H^1(M). ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

It does not name the set as GM(M), which is the paper’s notation for the set of generalized minimal flows on M. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

It leaves the meaning of 'proper subset' implicit. Here the intended statement is that GM(M) is nonempty and not equal to YU(M), i.e. GM(M) ≠ ∅ and GM(M) ⊊ YU(M). ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

It does not convey the nearby motivation: the paper explains that GM is already known to be nonempty in a weak-attractor sense, and known to be nontrivial for some special domains, which is exactly why Problem 13 asks for a uniform result for every compact analytic 2-manifold with analytic boundary. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
refined_question: Let M be a compact analytic Riemannian 2-manifold with analytic boundary, and let YU(M) be the Yudovich space of divergence-free vector fields u on M such that curl u ∈ L∞(M). Let S_t be the Euler flow on YU(M), let O(u) = {S_tu : t ∈ R} be the orbit of u, and let \bar O(u) be the weak closure of O(u) in H^1(M). Define u ∈ YU(M) to be a generalized minimal flow if every w ∈ \bar O(u) satisfies ||curl w||L2(M) = ||curl u||L2(M), and denote by GM(M) the set of all such flows. Prove that GM(M) is a nonempty proper subset of YU(M). ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
justification: The draft is not merely close to the paper; it is essentially a compressed version of Problem 13 in Section 6.3. The only substantive omissions are the paper’s definitions of YU(M), the Euler orbit/weak-closure notation, and Definition 6.7 of GM-flow. The neighboring Problem 14 concerns analyticity of vorticity level lines for GM-flows, and Problem 15 concerns the background region B0, so broadening to those would move away from the exact target. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))
